manifest.title: An array<array-key, int> argument cannot satisfy a parameter declared array<string, int>

ground_truth.statement: An array key is an int or a string and nothing else, and array-key is int|string, so an array declared array<array-key, int> is an array<int|string, int> and may contain int keys - the argument here contains the int key 0. The callee declares array<string, int> and applies strtoupper() to every key, which under strict_types fails with a TypeError on that int key. Passing an argument of type array<array-key, int> into a parameter of type array<string, int> is therefore unsound: the declared key type is a contract the argument cannot meet, and a diagnostic belongs on the call. PHP also normalises a numeric string key to int, so the caller cannot satisfy a string key type by spelling key 0 as '0' either.

phpstan.reason: PHPStan explicitly defines array-key as a permissive benevolent union rather than a strictly checked int|string alias. ArrayType normalizes that key to implicit mixed, and this baseline level-9 configuration leaves checkImplicitMixed disabled. Silence is therefore an excluded documented configuration-scope difference. An independent check with checkImplicitMixed: true emits argument.type on the unchanged fixture; the rule is implemented.

manifest.notes: This tests the array key contract, distinct from the element value contract. The runtime consequence remains real: an int key reaches strtoupper() under strict_types and throws. Psalm 6.20.0 and Mago 1.57.0 diagnose the call. The initial factory report counted PHPStan's level-9 silence as FN, but a later source and documentation audit corrected that classification without changing the fixture or its runtime result. This is a documented dialect/configuration difference, not a missing implemented check, and is excluded consistently with the optional PHPDoc signature check. The older immutable factory reports retain the original FN for audit history; use the corrected cohort report for current claims. ground_truth.statement: Shelter::adopt() documents @return Dog and BadShelter::adopt() documents @return Animal, returning a Cat. ground_truth.statement: Box declares @template T with @return T on get(), so the annotation @param Box<Cat> tells the caller that get() hands back a Cat, and the member access that follows has to be resolved against Cat - which has no bark(). manifest.title: A covariant template used in a parameter position makes the declared variance unsound

ground_truth.statement: Bag declares @template-covariant T, which promises that a Bag<Dog> may be used wherever a Bag<Animal> is expected, and it also declares push() with @param T, a write position. Those two promises cannot both hold. The runtime script executes the program the declarations license: put_cat() is typed Bag<Animal>, the covariant promise makes the caller's Bag<Dog> acceptable to it, put_cat() stores a Cat in that box, and the caller - whose annotation says Bag<Dog> - reads a Cat back. A Cat is not a Dog (the script checks the sibling relationship directly), and adopt() declares the native return type Dog, so the call fails with 'adopt(): Return value must be of type Dog, Cat returned'. A fresh Bag constructed with a Dog does read back a Dog, so the failure is caused by the declared write position and not by the widening on its own.

manifest.notes: The rule under test is the consistency of a declared generic variance: @template-covariant T means 'every reader of a Bag<Dog> may treat it as a Bag<Animal>', and that is sound only while T never appears in a write position. PHP has no generics, so the declaration itself cannot fail; what fails is the program the declaration grants, and the case's neutral ground truth for all three tools is that program. declare(strict_types=1);

// Runtime side of the ground truth. Bag declares @template-covariant T, so the
// declaration promises that a Bag<Dog> may be used wherever a Bag<Animal> is
// expected - that is what covariance buys the caller. It also declares push()
// with @param T, a write position. Those two promises cannot both hold: put_cat()
// accepts a Bag<Animal> and writes a Cat through that view, the original holder
// of a Bag<Dog> then reads a Cat where its annotation promises a Dog, and the
// native return type of adopt() enforces exactly that promise.

require __DIR__ . '/../src/repro.php';

use function Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition\adopt;
use function Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition\put_cat;
use function Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition\run;

use Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition\Bag;
use Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition\Cat;
use Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition\Dog;

// The sibling classes are unrelated: a Cat is not a Dog, so a Cat written into a
// Bag<Dog> makes the caller's guarantee false independently of any analyzer.
if ((new Cat()) instanceof Dog) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "Cat is a Dog; the fixture no longer witnesses the write\n");
    exit(1);
}

// The honest path: a fresh Bag<Dog> holding a Dog reads back a Dog.
$fresh = new Bag(new Dog());
if (!$fresh->get() instanceof Dog) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "a fresh Bag constructed with a Dog did not read back a Dog\n");
    exit(1);
}

// The write through the widened view: put_cat() is typed Bag<Animal>, which
// covariance makes the Bag<Dog> acceptable to, and it stores a Cat in the very
// box the caller annotated as Bag<Dog>.
$holder = new Bag(new Dog());
put_cat($holder);
if (!$holder->get() instanceof Cat) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "put_cat() did not write a Cat through the widened view\n");
    exit(1);
}

// return type, so the Cat that covariance let in reaches that return type and
// the call fails. This is the fact the case is about - the covariant
// declaration plus a write position is unsound, not merely unidiomatic.
$type_error = null;
try {
    run();
} catch (TypeError $error) {
    $type_error = $error;
}

if ($type_error === null) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "run() returned; the Cat did not reach adopt()'s Dog return type\n");
    exit(1);
}

if (strpos($type_error->getMessage(), 'adopt') === false
    || strpos($type_error->getMessage(), 'Dog') === false
    || strpos($type_error->getMessage(), 'Cat') === false) {
    fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("unexpected failure: %s\n", $type_error->getMessage()));
    exit(1);
}

printf(
    "put_cat() stored a Cat in a Bag<Dog> through the covariant widening; adopt() failed on its Dog return type: %s\n",
    $type_error->getMessage()
);
exit(0);

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition;

class Animal
{
}

final class Dog extends Animal
{
}

final class Cat extends Animal
{
}

/**
 * @template-covariant T
 */
final class Bag
{
    /** @param T $value */
    public function __construct(private mixed $value)
    {
    }

    /** @param T $value */
    public function push(mixed $value): void
    {
        $this->value = $value;
    }

    /** @return T */
    public function get(): mixed
    {
        return $this->value;
    }
}

/** @param Bag<Animal> $bag */
function put_cat(Bag $bag): void
{
    $bag->push(new Cat());
}

/** @param Bag<Dog> $dogs */
function adopt(Bag $dogs): Dog
{
    put_cat($dogs);

    return $dogs->get();
}

function run(): Dog
{
    return adopt(new Bag(new Dog()));
}

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Narrowing\IsNumericAfterIsInt;

/**
 * The right operand of && can never change the result once the left operand
 * has been evaluated: is_int($c) narrows $c to int, and is_numeric() is true
 * for every int. The second call is therefore redundant, and the whole
 * condition is decided by is_int($c) alone.
 */
function classify(int|string $c): string
{
    if (is_int($c) && is_numeric($c)) {
        return 'int';
    }

    return 'other';
}

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Nullability\ElseifElseReturnKeepsPossibleNull;

/**
 * Execution continues past the structure when at least one of the two
 * conditions held - not when both did. With $a !== null and $b === null the
 * first branch runs, $b was never tested, and the final check still has a true
 * outcome.
 */
function is_null_after(?string $a, ?string $b): bool
{
    if ($a !== null) {
        $a = trim($a);
    } elseif ($b !== null) {
        $b = trim($b);
    } else {
        return false;
    }

    return $b === null;
}

manifest.title: '' == null is true but '' === null is false, so the strict check inside the loose guard is not redundant

ground_truth.statement: In PHP 8, comparing null with a non-empty string is false and comparing it with '' is true, while '' === null is false. Inside the `$value == null` branch the value can therefore be '', so the inner `$value === null` has a reachable false outcome and the code behind it runs.

manifest.notes: The loose-null guard is a legacy defensive pattern. A tool that treats `== null` like `=== null` reports the inner check as redundant and the branch as dead; the runtime script shows both are alive. The '0' sample is a deliberate control: '0' == null is false and must not enter the outer branch. This string/null rule is not a PHP 8 change. The finding is independently corroborated by upstream report PR 2579 (https://github.com/carthage-software/mago/pull/2579), which describes the same root cause; the runtime proof here was derived from the fixture first.

namespace Bench\Nullability\RelationalComparisonExcludesNull;

function accept_int(int $_): void {}

/**
 * When null is compared with an integer, both operands convert to bool.
 * false > false is false, so null never enters the branch: inside it the
 * parameter is an int and accept_int() is satisfied.
 */
function quacks(?int $value): bool
{
    if ($value > 0) {
        accept_int($value);

        return true;
    }

    return false;
}
